title: Gold at $10,000 'Entirely Feasible', AI Trade Faces 'Implosion': Jefferies' Chris Wood
excerpt: In a CNBC-TV18 interview, Jefferies' Chris Wood laid out a scenario where US yield suppression sends gold past $10,000, warned of 'massive capital destruction' from AI spending, and called India a 'reverse AI trade' poised to benefit.
body:
• Jefferies strategist Chris Wood says gold at $10,000 an ounce is "entirely feasible" if the US is forced to suppress Treasury yields — a scenario that would "massively monetise Indian household balance sheets."
  • Wood warns the AI capex boom could end in "massive capital destruction" in the US, with hyperscaler spending unlikely to earn returns that justify it.
  • He argues the fastest way for foreign money to flood back into Indian equities is an "implosion" of the AI and semiconductor trade.
  • India is emerging as a "reverse AI trade," he says, with Indian IT firms positioned as enablers of enterprise AI adoption rather than its victims.

Jefferies' global head of equity strategy Chris Wood has laid out two of the boldest market calls on Wall Street: gold at $10,000 an ounce is "entirely feasible," and the AI capital-expenditure boom is heading for what he calls an "implosion" that could redirect global money back toward India.

Wood, author of the closely watched weekly note GREED & fear, made the remarks in an interview with CNBC-TV18, ranging across gold, US Treasury yields, the AI capex cycle, oil, and foreign investor flows into Indian equities.

The $10,000 gold call

Wood's gold thesis runs through the bond market. He believes Washington may eventually be forced to cap or suppress Treasury yields if pressures on the US debt market intensify — with federal debt now above $40 trillion and the 10-year yield touching 5%. Such yield suppression, he argues, would weaken the dollar and send gold soaring.

"Gold at $10,000 per ounce, which is entirely feasible in such an outcome, would massively monetise Indian household balance sheets," Wood said.

The Indian connection is the point. Indian households are among the largest private holders of gold in the world, and a more-than-doubling of the price from current levels near $4,300 would represent an enormous wealth transfer to ordinary savers — far beyond anything equity markets could deliver to the same households.

The AI "implosion" warning

Wood's darker call targets the defining trade of the decade: the hundreds of billions of dollars US hyperscalers are pouring into AI infrastructure. He questions whether the returns will ever justify the spending.

"My basic view is they're not going to make a return to justify these investments. My base case there'll be massive loss of capital destruction in the US," he said.

The cycle can continue, Wood conceded, for as long as markets keep funding it — but that willingness can vanish fast. "What will end this story very quickly is if the market suddenly decides to withdraw the credit card and say, 'We're not funding this anymore.'"

"The quickest way foreign money will return in size to the Indian stock market will be if the semiconductor cycle, the AI capex cycle, implodes."

— Chris Wood, Global Head of Equity Strategy, Jefferies

Why India could win the rotation

Wood's India argument follows directly from the AI warning. The AI and semiconductor trade has been vacuuming up global emerging-market capital, starving Indian equities of foreign flows. A sharp reversal — "implosion" is his word — would send that money hunting for relatively cheaper markets that lagged the boom.

"MSCI China is one obvious area of mean reversion rotating out of AI plays in Asia, as is India," Wood wrote in GREED & fear, describing a broader move away from momentum-driven AI trades. He cited Tencent as an example in Asia, and noted that conversations around "AI fatigue" have become more prominent as investors question whether gains in AI-linked companies have become stretched.

He pointed to South Korea as a cautionary tale: AI-linked shares there rallied exorbitantly before coming down sharply, in what he called "hyperbolic moves."

Indian IT: from victims to enablers

Wood also pushed back on the consensus that artificial intelligence is an existential threat to India's $250-billion IT services industry, which employs around 5.8 million people. The sector has significantly underperformed both domestic and emerging-market peers on exactly that fear.

But enterprise demand for AI implementation is real, Wood argues — and Indian firms are positioned to capture it. Infosys disclosed that 90% of its top 200 large clients are already using its AI services, and the company recently unveiled an "AI First" services strategy in Bengaluru that Jefferies estimates could address a $300-400 billion market opportunity by 2030.

"This matters from a market perspective because it challenges the assumption that Indian IT services are inevitable losers from AI, which has been a key reason for their severe underperformance," Wood wrote. He prefers AI infrastructure firms over the hyperscalers themselves, given his doubts about monetisation at the top of the stack.

What to watch

Wood's calls are scenarios, not forecasts with dates attached — and he acknowledged the AI cycle is not over, with some correction in AI stocks "both expected and healthy" after the run-up. The triggers to watch are concrete: any US move toward yield suppression, a funding freeze in the hyperscaler capex pipeline, and the direction of foreign institutional flows into Indian equities. If the AI trade cracks, Wood's "reverse AI trade" — India included — is where he says the money goes next.
image_caption: Christopher Wood, global head of equity strategy at Jefferies. Wood says gold at $10,000 an ounce is 'entirely feasible' and warns the AI capex boom could end in 'massive capital destruction.'
nri_angle: Wood's thesis ties two of the biggest market debates directly to Indian households and portfolios: a gold surge would massively enrich Indian savers, and an AI-trade reversal would bring foreign flows back to Indian equities.
